payload.title: Rhetorical Analysis: A Veteran River Guide Addresses the New Class
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Remarks to the First-Year Guides
Marisol Tenney, spring orientation address, Hollis Bend Outfitters, 2019 (fictional)

¶1 (1) Twenty-seven springs ago I stood where you are standing, in borrowed sandals, certain that I already understood the river. (2) I had run the Corrow four times as a passenger. (3) I could name every rapid between the put-in and Saddler's Gate. (4) What I could not do, and did not know I could not do, was read water. (5) That is the gap I want to talk about this morning, because it is the gap that puts people in the hospital.

¶2 (6) Reading water is not memorizing a map. (7) A map tells you where the rock was last August; the river tells you where the rock is right now, and it tells you only if you are watching. (8) Look downstream of any boulder and you will see a pillow of smooth water piled against its upstream face, a seam of folded current along its shoulder, and a tongue of dark green pointing the way through. (9) The pillow warns, the seam steers, the tongue invites. (10) Those three signs say more than any guidebook, and they change every hour as the gauge rises or falls. (11) The river is a sentence that rewrites itself while you are reading it.

¶3 (12) I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too. (13) You are strong, you are quick, and you have the kind of balance that makes a raft feel like a living room floor. (14) Fine. (15) Strength matters, and I will not pretend otherwise. (16) But strength gets you out of trouble that reading would have kept you out of altogether, and the river does not grade on effort. (17) In my fourth season a guide named Ollie Brask, stronger than any of us, high-sided too late at Kettle Drop because he was looking at his paddle instead of the pillow. (18) Six people swam. (19) One of them, a schoolteacher from Dunmore, spent eleven days with a tube in her chest. (20) Ollie never guided again, not because we sent him away but because he could not forgive himself for the second and a half he spent not looking.

¶4 (21) So here is the arithmetic of this job. (22) Last season Hollis Bend ran 1,140 commercial trips. (23) On 1,137 of them nobody got hurt beyond a scraped shin. (24) That sounds like success, and in most trades it would be. (25) On a river it means three families went home carrying a story they did not sign up for, and each of those stories has a guide's name in it. (26) You will not be judged by the thousand quiet days. (27) You will be judged by the one loud one, and you should be.

¶5 (28) Humility, in this work, is not a mood; it is a procedure. (29) It is scouting a rapid you have run three hundred times because the water came up two inches overnight. (30) It is saying out loud, in front of the guests, "I am not sure, let's eddy out and look," when every part of you wants to seem certain. (31) It is admitting that the river has a longer memory than you do and a shorter temper.

¶6 (32) Who sits in your boat? (33) A retired welder who saved for two years. (34) A nine-year-old who has not yet decided whether she is brave. (35) A father who will never say so but is more afraid of the water than she is. (36) They have handed you something they cannot get back, and they did it on the strength of a company brochure and the fact that you looked at them and smiled. (37) Honor that.

¶7 (38) I will not tell you the river is your enemy; it is not. (39) It is indifferent, which is harder, because an enemy at least pays attention to you. (40) So you will pay attention for both of you. (41) Watch the pillow. (42) Trust the tongue. (43) Scout when in doubt, and be in doubt more often than feels comfortable. (44) The Corrow was carving this canyon before anyone was here to name it, and it will go on rewriting itself long after the last of us has pulled a boat out at Saddler's Gate. (45) Read it as if your passengers' lives depend on it, because on the loud day, they do.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Speaker: Marisol Tenney, a fictional guide with twenty-seven seasons on the fictional Corrow River. Audience: a dozen first-year guides at the spring orientation of Hollis Bend Outfitters, a fictional rafting company, in 2019. Exigence: the new guides are physically capable but have not yet learned to read moving water, and the company has had three injuries in the previous season. Purpose: to persuade the new guides that reading water, practiced humility, and a felt sense of responsibility for passengers matter more than strength or confidence, and to get them to adopt specific habits (scouting, admitting uncertainty, watching the surface) before the season begins.

The passage below is the text of remarks delivered by Marisol Tenney, a veteran river guide, to a group of first-year guides at a spring orientation held by Hollis Bend Outfitters in 2019. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Tenney makes to convince the new guides that attentiveness and humility, not strength or confidence, are what keep passengers safe.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of how Tenney's rhetorical choices serve her purpose.
- Select and present specific evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
- Explain in your commentary how the evidence you cite shows the choices working on the audience and advancing Tenney's purpose.
parts.model_answer:
Tenney's audience is a room full of people who have probably never been told they aren't good enough at something physical. They are strong, quick, and new, and that combination is exactly what makes them dangerous. Tenney can't just order them to be humble, because confident first-year guides will hear "be humble" as "be weak." So she builds her speech to make humility look like a skill instead of a personality trait, and a skill she herself once lacked. By opening with her own overconfidence, conceding the value of strength before showing its limits, and saving the passengers' faces for after the technical lesson, Tenney makes attentiveness feel both learnable and morally required.

Her first move is to stand where the new guides stand. She could have used her twenty-seven seasons as a credential, but she uses them to show how long ago she was wrong, "certain that I already understood the river." Being able to "name every rapid" is something a new guide might brag about, and she sets it up only to knock it down: "What I could not do, and did not know I could not do, was read water." The repetition puts the weight on the not knowing. This lets her criticize the guides without insulting them. If the expert was once this ignorant, ignorance isn't shameful, but staying that way is.

Paragraph 2 then hands them something concrete. After describing the boulder, she compresses it into "The pillow warns, the seam steers, the tongue invites." The parallel structure works almost like a drill, easy to remember on the water in a few weeks. But she follows it with "The river is a sentence that rewrites itself while you are reading it," which turns the lesson against memorizing. Confidence built on past runs is useless if the river changes every hour, and that sets up her real argument.

Only now does she deal with strength, and she is careful about it. "Fine. Strength matters, and I will not pretend otherwise" gives the guides what they are proud of, but the one-word "Fine" sounds like a shrug. She respects their strength without being impressed by it. Her rebuttal recasts strength as a backup plan, something that "gets you out of trouble that reading would have kept you out of altogether." The Ollie Brask story proves the point, and she picks a guide "stronger than any of us" on purpose so nobody in the room can think they're the exception. "Six people swam" is flat and undramatic, which makes it worse, and the schoolteacher with "a tube in her chest" makes the cost physical.

The statistics could have made the company look good, but Tenney flips them: "You will be judged by the one loud one, and you should be." That last clause shuts down any complaint about fairness. Then she defines humility as "a procedure," like scouting a rapid "you have run three hundred times." For people who want to do something with their strength, this works, because humility becomes an action and not a feeling of being small.

The passengers come last, and that ordering matters. If "Who sits in your boat?" had opened the speech, the welder and the nine-year-old would only produce vague guilt. Coming after the pillow and the procedure, the emotion attaches to habits the guides now know how to perform. The girl "who has not yet decided whether she is brave" suggests a guide's choices shape more than physical safety. When Tenney says the river is "indifferent" and "you will pay attention for both of you," the job grows from reading water to carrying trust. So her closing commands, "Watch the pillow. Trust the tongue," repeat the first lesson, but by now they carry everything that came after.

rubric_rows.criterion: Counts as defensible: any thesis tying one or more named choices to the purpose of making attentiveness and humility feel more urgent than strength or confidence. A thesis that merely lists three devices without saying what they do for her purpose earns 0.

Choices that count include: the opening ethos of twenty-seven seasons and the admission in sentence 4; the extended metaphor of the river as a sentence that rewrites itself (11, 44); the enumeration and parallelism of pillow, seam, tongue (8-9, 41-42); the concession about strength and its rebuttal (12-16); the Ollie Brask anecdote with its short sentence 18; the statistics reframed in 22-27; the definition of humility as procedure (28-31); the rhetorical question and the catalog of passengers (32-37); the personification of an indifferent river (38-40); the tone shifts between instruction, warning, and tenderness. Full credit does not require covering all of these.

Do not award this point for merely noting that the speech 'uses ethos, pathos, and logos' or for ornate vocabulary. Award it for a sustained explanation of how the speech works as a whole on a specific audience of capable but inexperienced listeners.

payload.reference_text:
Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). Each essay is worth 6 points.
Thesis (0-1): Counts as defensible: any thesis tying one or more named choices to the purpose of making attentiveness and humility feel more urgent than strength or confidence. A thesis that merely lists three devices without saying what they do for her purpose earns 0.
   - 1: A defensible claim about how Tenney's choices work on the new guides. The claim may be a single sentence anywhere in the essay. It must name at least one identifiable move or pattern (an anecdote, a shift from instruction to warning, the redefinition of humility, the catalog of passengers, the concession about strength) and connect it to her aim of changing how the guides think or behave.
   - 0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Tenney uses rhetorical choices to convince the guides'), or one that summarizes the speech, or one that argues about river safety itself rather than about how the speech works.
Evidence and Commentary (0-4): Choices that count include: the opening ethos of twenty-seven seasons and the admission in sentence 4; the extended metaphor of the river as a sentence that rewrites itself (11, 44); the enumeration and parallelism of pillow, seam, tongue (8-9, 41-42); the concession about strength and its rebuttal (12-16); the Ollie Brask anecdote with its short sentence 18; the statistics reframed in 22-27; the definition of humility as procedure (28-31); the rhetorical question and the catalog of passengers (32-37); the personification of an indifferent river (38-40); the tone shifts between instruction, warning, and tenderness. Full credit does not require covering all of these.
   - 4: Sustains a line of reasoning across the essay: evidence is consistently well chosen and the commentary explains not only what each choice does but why Tenney makes it at that moment for these listeners. The essay accounts for the movement of the speech (for instance, from the technical lesson of paragraph two to the anecdote, the statistics, the redefinition of humility, and the closing catalog of passengers) and shows how choices build on each other.
   - 3: Supplies specific evidence for each claim and explains how at least two or three choices advance Tenney's purpose with this audience (new, strong, overconfident guides). Commentary follows the evidence rather than preceding it. Some explanations may be uneven, and the essay may not account for the shift in the passage or for how choices work together.
   - 2: Identifies some rhetorical choices with accurate evidence (for example, names the Ollie Brask anecdote or the 1,140 trips figure) but commentary mostly labels the device or states its effect in one sentence without explaining how it works on first-year guides specifically. Reasoning may be a list of devices rather than a line of argument.
   - 1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of what Tenney says, with general comments such as 'this makes the audience feel emotional' that could be said of any passage. Evidence may be quoted but is not tied to a choice.
   - 0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the speech, or offers no evidence from the passage.
Sophistication (0-1): Do not award this point for merely noting that the speech 'uses ethos, pathos, and logos' or for ornate vocabulary. Award it for a sustained explanation of how the speech works as a whole on a specific audience of capable but inexperienced listeners.
   - 1: The essay does one or more of the following consistently and in support of its argument: explains the tension Tenney manages between respecting the guides' strength and undercutting their confidence; explains why she positions responsibility (the passengers) after the technical lesson rather than before it; notices how she makes herself an example of the overconfidence she warns against and why that matters for credibility; or writes with precise, controlled prose throughout that advances the analysis.
   - 0: Commentary stays at the level of naming devices and effects; prose is serviceable but general; or the essay makes sweeping claims about rhetoric in general or inflates its language without adding insight.
Note: Total is the sum of rows A, B, and C (maximum 6).
Note: An essay that earns 0 on row A can still earn up to 2 on row B if it accurately discusses choices in the passage; it cannot earn row C.
Note: Essays that mislabel a device (calling the anecdote a statistic, for instance) but accurately explain its effect should not be penalized for the label.
Note: Essays that treat the passage as an argument to agree or disagree with rather than analyzing its rhetoric are capped at 1 on row B.
Note: Quotation is not required; precise paraphrase with sentence references is acceptable evidence.

   - "By opening with her own overconfidence, conceding the value of strength before showing its limits, and saving the passengers' faces for after the technical lesson, Tenney makes attentiveness feel both learnable and morally required." - Defensible thesis. It names specific choices (self-example, concession, the ordering of the passengers) and ties them to her purpose of changing how the guides think. It also sets up the line of reasoning the essay follows.
   - "The repetition puts the weight on the not knowing. This lets her criticize the guides without insulting them." - Commentary comes after the evidence and explains how the opening admission works on this audience in particular, not just what the device is called.
   - "which turns the lesson against memorizing" - Links the metaphor to the parallelism before it and to the argument against confidence that comes next. This shows choices building on each other.
   - "she picks a guide "stronger than any of us" on purpose so nobody in the room can think they're the exception" - Explains why the anecdote fits strong, overconfident listeners. Analysis of purpose, not plot summary.
   - "That last clause shuts down any complaint about fairness." - Reads the reframed statistics closely and explains their persuasive work. The essay follows the speech in order from lesson to anecdote to numbers to humility to passengers, which earns the top score for row B.
   - "She respects their strength without being impressed by it." - Part of a sustained explanation of the tension Tenney manages between honoring the guides' strength and undercutting their confidence. It starts in the introduction and carries through the essay.
   - "The passengers come last, and that ordering matters." - Explains why responsibility comes after the technical lesson rather than before it, one of the rubric's named moves for sophistication. The essay develops this point instead of just stating it.
   - "If the expert was once this ignorant, ignorance isn't shameful, but staying that way is." - Notices that Tenney makes herself an example of the overconfidence she warns against and explains why that helps her credibility. Together with the other moves, this makes the sophistication sustained.

Sample response, middle score (4/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 3, Sophistication 0):
In her remarks to the new guides, Marisol Tenney uses a personal admission, a story about another guide, and a definition of humility to make the guides see that paying attention is more important than being strong or sure of themselves. She does this by first earning their trust and then slowly making the stakes feel real.

Tenney begins by telling the guides she was once just like them. She says "Twenty-seven springs ago I stood where you are standing, in borrowed sandals, certain that I already understood the river." This is a smart choice because the audience is made up of capable, confident people who might not listen to an older person lecturing them. By admitting that she "could name every rapid" but "could not do" what mattered, which was read water, she shows that her twenty-seven seasons come with a mistake attached. The guides can believe her because she is not claiming to have been perfect. It also sets up the gap between knowing the river and reading it, which the rest of the speech depends on.

After the lesson on pillows, seams, and tongues, Tenney takes on the guides' pride directly. She says "I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too," and then agrees that strength matters before saying that "strength gets you out of trouble that reading would have kept you out of altogether." The concession keeps the guides from getting defensive, and then the rebuttal turns their strength into something that is not enough on its own. Right after this she tells the story of Ollie Brask, who was "stronger than any of us" but looked at his paddle instead of the pillow. The anecdote has a short sentence, "Six people swam," that hits hard after the longer ones. The detail about the schoolteacher with a tube in her chest makes the danger real instead of just a warning. Since Ollie was strong, the guides cannot say that it would not happen to them.

Tenney then uses numbers. She says 1,137 of 1,140 trips went fine, but that the three bad ones mean "three families went home carrying a story they did not sign up for." This changes how the guides think about success, because the number that sounds good is made to sound like a failure. It also connects to the three injuries the company had last season, which the guides would know about.

Next she defines humility as "a procedure," not "a mood." This gives the guides actual habits like scouting and saying "I am not sure," which is what she wants them to do. Finally the question "Who sits in your boat?" lists a welder, a nine-year-old, and a father. These examples make the guides feel responsible, and the ending line about the "loud day" brings back the earlier statistics. Overall the speech moves from trust, to warning, to instruction, to feeling, so that the guides leave wanting to be careful instead of just being told to.
   - "Tenney uses a personal admission, a story about another guide, and a definition of humility to make the guides see that paying attention is more important than being strong or sure of themselves." - Defensible thesis: names specific moves (admission, anecdote, redefinition of humility) and ties them to changing how the guides think. Earns the thesis point, though it is a bit loosely worded.
   - "By admitting that she "could name every rapid" but "could not do" what mattered, which was read water, she shows that her twenty-seven seasons come with a mistake attached." - Accurate evidence with commentary on why the admission builds credibility with overconfident listeners. This is the strongest analysis in the essay, but it does not push further on why the admission comes first.
   - "The concession keeps the guides from getting defensive, and then the rebuttal turns their strength into something that is not enough on its own." - Explains the concession and rebuttal and how they work on this audience. Touches on the tension between respecting strength and undercutting confidence but only briefly, so it does not reach sophistication.
   - "The anecdote has a short sentence, "Six people swam," that hits hard after the longer ones." - Identifies the short sentence but the commentary is general ("hits hard") and does not explain how the sentence works on the guides.
   - "This changes how the guides think about success, because the number that sounds good is made to sound like a failure." - Good point about the statistics being reframed, but explanation is brief and not tied closely to the audience's pride or to the thesis.
   - "These examples make the guides feel responsible, and the ending line about the "loud day" brings back the earlier statistics." - Notes a link back to the statistics, but the catalog of passengers is mostly labeled rather than explained, and the conclusion summarizes the speech's order instead of showing how the choices build on each other.

Sample response, low score (2/6; Thesis 0, Evidence and commentary 2, Sophistication 0):
In her speech to the new guides Marisol Tenney uses many rhetorical choices to convince them that being attentive and humble is more important than being strong. She uses stories, statistics, and strong language to get her point across to the audience and make them want to change.

Tenney starts by talking about herself. She says "Twenty-seven springs ago I stood where you are standing" and that she was certain she understood the river. This shows she has been a guide for a long time so the new guides will listen to her. It also shows that she was once like them, so they might relate to her.

Then she explains what reading water is with the pillow, seam, and tongue. She says "The pillow warns, the seam steers, the tongue invites." This is repeated later when she says watch the pillow and trust the tongue. The repetition helps the guides remember it. She also says the river is a sentence that rewrites itself, which is a metaphor and shows that the river is always changing.

Next she tells the story about Ollie Brask. He was strong but he looked at his paddle and six people swam. A schoolteacher had a tube in her chest. This story is sad and makes the audience feel bad, so they will see that strength is not enough. It is a good example because it is a real consequence of not paying attention.

She also uses numbers. She says Hollis Bend ran 1,140 trips and in 1,137 nobody got hurt. But she says the three that did get hurt matter. This makes the guides see that even a few injuries is a big deal.

At the end she asks "Who sits in your boat?" and lists a welder, a nine-year-old, and a father. This makes the guides think about the passengers and feel responsible. Her last line says to read the river as if lives depend on it. Overall Tenney's choices work together to persuade the guides to be humble and pay attention.
   - "This shows she has been a guide for a long time so the new guides will listen to her." - Identifies ethos accurately but does not note that her admission of past overconfidence is what makes her credible to overconfident listeners; commentary is one general sentence.
   - "The repetition helps the guides remember it." - Labels the parallelism and gives a generic effect without explaining why the technical lesson comes first or how it works on these listeners.
   - "This story is sad and makes the audience feel bad, so they will see that strength is not enough." - Right evidence (Ollie Brask) but the commentary is a vague emotional claim that could fit any passage; it misses the short sentence and the concession about strength.
   - "Overall Tenney's choices work together to persuade the guides to be humble and pay attention." - The conclusion repeats the prompt and the essay never explains the movement of the speech or the tension between respecting strength and undercutting confidence, so no sophistication.

(44) The Corrow was carving this canyon before anyone was here to name it, and it will go on rewriting itself long after the last of us has pulled a boat out at Saddler's Gate.
(45) Read it as if your passengers' lives depend on it, because on the loud day, they do.
sources.stance: Reading water, humility, and responsibility for passengers outweigh strength and confidence.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Tenney uses rhetorical choices to convince the guides'), or one that summarizes the speech, or one that argues about river safety itself rather than about how the speech works.
descriptors.1: A defensible claim about how Tenney's choices work on the new guides. The claim may be a single sentence anywhere in the essay. It must name at least one identifiable move or pattern (an anecdote, a shift from instruction to warning, the redefinition of humility, the catalog of passengers, the concession about strength) and connect it to her aim of changing how the guides think or behave.

rows.task_specific: Counts as defensible: any thesis tying one or more named choices to the purpose of making attentiveness and humility feel more urgent than strength or confidence. A thesis that merely lists three devices without saying what they do for her purpose earns 0.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the speech, or offers no evidence from the passage.
descriptors.1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of what Tenney says, with general comments such as 'this makes the audience feel emotional' that could be said of any passage. Evidence may be quoted but is not tied to a choice.
descriptors.2: Identifies some rhetorical choices with accurate evidence (for example, names the Ollie Brask anecdote or the 1,140 trips figure) but commentary mostly labels the device or states its effect in one sentence without explaining how it works on first-year guides specifically. Reasoning may be a list of devices rather than a line of argument.
descriptors.3: Supplies specific evidence for each claim and explains how at least two or three choices advance Tenney's purpose with this audience (new, strong, overconfident guides). Commentary follows the evidence rather than preceding it. Some explanations may be uneven, and the essay may not account for the shift in the passage or for how choices work together.
descriptors.4: Sustains a line of reasoning across the essay: evidence is consistently well chosen and the commentary explains not only what each choice does but why Tenney makes it at that moment for these listeners. The essay accounts for the movement of the speech (for instance, from the technical lesson of paragraph two to the anecdote, the statistics, the redefinition of humility, and the closing catalog of passengers) and shows how choices build on each other.

rows.task_specific: Choices that count include: the opening ethos of twenty-seven seasons and the admission in sentence 4; the extended metaphor of the river as a sentence that rewrites itself (11, 44); the enumeration and parallelism of pillow, seam, tongue (8-9, 41-42); the concession about strength and its rebuttal (12-16); the Ollie Brask anecdote with its short sentence 18; the statistics reframed in 22-27; the definition of humility as procedure (28-31); the rhetorical question and the catalog of passengers (32-37); the personification of an indifferent river (38-40); the tone shifts between instruction, warning, and tenderness. Full credit does not require covering all of these.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Commentary stays at the level of naming devices and effects; prose is serviceable but general; or the essay makes sweeping claims about rhetoric in general or inflates its language without adding insight.
descriptors.1: The essay does one or more of the following consistently and in support of its argument: explains the tension Tenney manages between respecting the guides' strength and undercutting their confidence; explains why she positions responsibility (the passengers) after the technical lesson rather than before it; notices how she makes herself an example of the overconfidence she warns against and why that matters for credibility; or writes with precise, controlled prose throughout that advances the analysis.

rows.task_specific: Do not award this point for merely noting that the speech 'uses ethos, pathos, and logos' or for ornate vocabulary. Award it for a sustained explanation of how the speech works as a whole on a specific audience of capable but inexperienced listeners.

scoring_notes: Total is the sum of rows A, B, and C (maximum 6).
An essay that earns 0 on row A can still earn up to 2 on row B if it accurately discusses choices in the passage; it cannot earn row C.
Essays that mislabel a device (calling the anecdote a statistic, for instance) but accurately explain its effect should not be penalized for the label.
Essays that treat the passage as an argument to agree or disagree with rather than analyzing its rhetoric are capped at 1 on row B.
Quotation is not required; precise paraphrase with sentence references is acceptable evidence.

defensible_positions: Tenney first earns the guides' trust by confessing her own early overconfidence, then uses concrete sensory instruction, a cautionary anecdote, and a reframed statistic to replace their faith in strength with a habit of watching.
The speech moves from the technical to the moral: by defining humility as a procedure and then naming the people in the boat, Tenney turns an abstract virtue into daily behavior with human stakes.
Tenney's concession that strength matters allows her to disarm the audience's likely resistance before she undercuts it with evidence that strength failed a stronger guide than any of them.
lines_of_reasoning: Ethos through confession (1-5) sets up the lesson in reading water (6-11), which the anecdote (17-20) proves necessary and the statistic (22-27) proves urgent; the definition (28-31) and catalog (32-37) then convert urgency into practice and responsibility.

Tenney anticipates and manages the audience's pride: the concession and blunt 'Fine' (12-16) acknowledge their strength, the anecdote shows its limits, and the closing imperatives (41-43) give them something to do with their energy instead.

Short sentences at moments of consequence (14, 18, 37, 41-42) punctuate longer explanatory sentences, so the rhythm of the speech itself enacts the alternation between watching and acting that she asks of the guides.

rhetorical_choices.effect: By admitting she once mistook familiarity for understanding, Tenney establishes both long experience and humility, modeling the attitude she will ask for and preempting the guides' sense that she cannot understand their confidence.
Naming pillow, seam, and tongue gives the guides a concrete vocabulary for watching, making 'reading water' a learnable skill rather than a vague ideal.
The three-part verb pattern makes the signs memorable and suggests the river communicates in an orderly grammar, preparing the metaphor that follows.
The river as a self-rewriting sentence frames guiding as continual reading, and its return in sentence 44 ties the technical lesson to the closing demand for lifelong attention.
Acknowledging the guides' strength lowers their defenses so that the rebuttal, that the river does not grade on effort, lands as fair rather than dismissive.

Ollie Brask, stronger than anyone, failing because of a second and a half of inattention, is a specific proof that strength cannot substitute for reading, and his guilt previews the moral weight of the job.
The one-word 'Fine' and the three-word 'Six people swam' stop the speech cold, giving the consequences a blunt finality the longer sentences cannot.
The near-perfect record is introduced only to be reread as three families harmed, teaching the guides to count by the loud day rather than the quiet ones.
Quiet days against the loud one condenses the lesson of the numbers into a standard the guides can carry, and 'you should be' closes off any objection that the standard is unfair.
Recasting humility as a procedure rather than a mood turns a character trait into specific actions (scouting, saying 'I am not sure'), which is what an orientation can actually ask for.
Asking who sits in the boat shifts the guides' attention from themselves to their passengers and sets up the catalog that answers it.

Three sharply particular passengers make trust tangible; the reminder that they trusted a brochure and a smile places the weight of that trust directly on the listener before the two-word command 'Honor that.'
Denying the river is an enemy and calling it indifferent removes any drama of combat and leaves the guide solely responsible for attention.

The speech moves from patient instruction to stern arithmetic to tenderness to crisp imperatives, so the guides experience in turn the knowledge, the fear, the care, and the habit she wants them to hold.
Closing imperatives return the guides to the vocabulary of paragraph two and convert the whole speech into instructions they can act on tomorrow.

source_uses.usable_for: All evidence; students should cite sentence numbers or quote directly.

common_pitfalls: Writing a device-list essay (one paragraph on ethos, one on pathos, one on logos) with no line of reasoning connecting them to the audience of new guides.
Summarizing the Ollie Brask story at length without explaining why Tenney places it immediately after conceding that strength matters.

Calling the passenger catalog in paragraph six 'emotional appeal' without explaining what the specificity (a welder's savings, a child's undecided bravery, a father's hidden fear) accomplishes for a speaker trying to make responsibility feel concrete.
Treating the 1,140 trips figure as simple logos while missing that Tenney reverses its apparent meaning in sentences 24-27.
Ignoring the speaker's own admitted overconfidence in sentences 1-4 and therefore missing how she builds credibility.
Arguing about whether river guiding is dangerous instead of analyzing the speech.

samples.essay:
Tenney's audience is a room full of people who have probably never been told they aren't good enough at something physical. They are strong, quick, and new, and that combination is exactly what makes them dangerous. Tenney can't just order them to be humble, because confident first-year guides will hear "be humble" as "be weak." So she builds her speech to make humility look like a skill instead of a personality trait, and a skill she herself once lacked. By opening with her own overconfidence, conceding the value of strength before showing its limits, and saving the passengers' faces for after the technical lesson, Tenney makes attentiveness feel both learnable and morally required.

Her first move is to stand where the new guides stand. She could have used her twenty-seven seasons as a credential, but she uses them to show how long ago she was wrong, "certain that I already understood the river." Being able to "name every rapid" is something a new guide might brag about, and she sets it up only to knock it down: "What I could not do, and did not know I could not do, was read water." The repetition puts the weight on the not knowing. This lets her criticize the guides without insulting them. If the expert was once this ignorant, ignorance isn't shameful, but staying that way is.

Paragraph 2 then hands them something concrete. After describing the boulder, she compresses it into "The pillow warns, the seam steers, the tongue invites." The parallel structure works almost like a drill, easy to remember on the water in a few weeks. But she follows it with "The river is a sentence that rewrites itself while you are reading it," which turns the lesson against memorizing. Confidence built on past runs is useless if the river changes every hour, and that sets up her real argument.

Only now does she deal with strength, and she is careful about it. "Fine. Strength matters, and I will not pretend otherwise" gives the guides what they are proud of, but the one-word "Fine" sounds like a shrug. She respects their strength without being impressed by it. Her rebuttal recasts strength as a backup plan, something that "gets you out of trouble that reading would have kept you out of altogether." The Ollie Brask story proves the point, and she picks a guide "stronger than any of us" on purpose so nobody in the room can think they're the exception. "Six people swam" is flat and undramatic, which makes it worse, and the schoolteacher with "a tube in her chest" makes the cost physical.

The statistics could have made the company look good, but Tenney flips them: "You will be judged by the one loud one, and you should be." That last clause shuts down any complaint about fairness. Then she defines humility as "a procedure," like scouting a rapid "you have run three hundred times." For people who want to do something with their strength, this works, because humility becomes an action and not a feeling of being small.

The passengers come last, and that ordering matters. If "Who sits in your boat?" had opened the speech, the welder and the nine-year-old would only produce vague guilt. Coming after the pillow and the procedure, the emotion attaches to habits the guides now know how to perform. The girl "who has not yet decided whether she is brave" suggests a guide's choices shape more than physical safety. When Tenney says the river is "indifferent" and "you will pay attention for both of you," the job grows from reading water to carrying trust. So her closing commands, "Watch the pillow. Trust the tongue," repeat the first lesson, but by now they carry everything that came after.

annotations.comment: Defensible thesis. It names specific choices (self-example, concession, the ordering of the passengers) and ties them to her purpose of changing how the guides think. It also sets up the line of reasoning the essay follows.

samples.essay:
In her remarks to the new guides, Marisol Tenney uses a personal admission, a story about another guide, and a definition of humility to make the guides see that paying attention is more important than being strong or sure of themselves. She does this by first earning their trust and then slowly making the stakes feel real.

Tenney begins by telling the guides she was once just like them. She says "Twenty-seven springs ago I stood where you are standing, in borrowed sandals, certain that I already understood the river." This is a smart choice because the audience is made up of capable, confident people who might not listen to an older person lecturing them. By admitting that she "could name every rapid" but "could not do" what mattered, which was read water, she shows that her twenty-seven seasons come with a mistake attached. The guides can believe her because she is not claiming to have been perfect. It also sets up the gap between knowing the river and reading it, which the rest of the speech depends on.

After the lesson on pillows, seams, and tongues, Tenney takes on the guides' pride directly. She says "I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too," and then agrees that strength matters before saying that "strength gets you out of trouble that reading would have kept you out of altogether." The concession keeps the guides from getting defensive, and then the rebuttal turns their strength into something that is not enough on its own. Right after this she tells the story of Ollie Brask, who was "stronger than any of us" but looked at his paddle instead of the pillow. The anecdote has a short sentence, "Six people swam," that hits hard after the longer ones. The detail about the schoolteacher with a tube in her chest makes the danger real instead of just a warning. Since Ollie was strong, the guides cannot say that it would not happen to them.

Tenney then uses numbers. She says 1,137 of 1,140 trips went fine, but that the three bad ones mean "three families went home carrying a story they did not sign up for." This changes how the guides think about success, because the number that sounds good is made to sound like a failure. It also connects to the three injuries the company had last season, which the guides would know about.

Next she defines humility as "a procedure," not "a mood." This gives the guides actual habits like scouting and saying "I am not sure," which is what she wants them to do. Finally the question "Who sits in your boat?" lists a welder, a nine-year-old, and a father. These examples make the guides feel responsible, and the ending line about the "loud day" brings back the earlier statistics. Overall the speech moves from trust, to warning, to instruction, to feeling, so that the guides leave wanting to be careful instead of just being told to.

annotations.quote: Tenney uses a personal admission, a story about another guide, and a definition of humility to make the guides see that paying attention is more important than being strong or sure of themselves.
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis: names specific moves (admission, anecdote, redefinition of humility) and ties them to changing how the guides think. Earns the thesis point, though it is a bit loosely worded.

annotations.quote: By admitting that she "could name every rapid" but "could not do" what mattered, which was read water, she shows that her twenty-seven seasons come with a mistake attached.
annotations.comment: Accurate evidence with commentary on why the admission builds credibility with overconfident listeners. This is the strongest analysis in the essay, but it does not push further on why the admission comes first.

annotations.quote: The concession keeps the guides from getting defensive, and then the rebuttal turns their strength into something that is not enough on its own.
annotations.comment: Explains the concession and rebuttal and how they work on this audience. Touches on the tension between respecting strength and undercutting confidence but only briefly, so it does not reach sophistication.

annotations.quote: The anecdote has a short sentence, "Six people swam," that hits hard after the longer ones.
annotations.comment: Identifies the short sentence but the commentary is general ("hits hard") and does not explain how the sentence works on the guides.

annotations.quote: This changes how the guides think about success, because the number that sounds good is made to sound like a failure.
annotations.comment: Good point about the statistics being reframed, but explanation is brief and not tied closely to the audience's pride or to the thesis.

samples.essay:
In her speech to the new guides Marisol Tenney uses many rhetorical choices to convince them that being attentive and humble is more important than being strong. She uses stories, statistics, and strong language to get her point across to the audience and make them want to change.

Tenney starts by talking about herself. She says "Twenty-seven springs ago I stood where you are standing" and that she was certain she understood the river. This shows she has been a guide for a long time so the new guides will listen to her. It also shows that she was once like them, so they might relate to her.

Then she explains what reading water is with the pillow, seam, and tongue. She says "The pillow warns, the seam steers, the tongue invites." This is repeated later when she says watch the pillow and trust the tongue. The repetition helps the guides remember it. She also says the river is a sentence that rewrites itself, which is a metaphor and shows that the river is always changing.

Next she tells the story about Ollie Brask. He was strong but he looked at his paddle and six people swam. A schoolteacher had a tube in her chest. This story is sad and makes the audience feel bad, so they will see that strength is not enough. It is a good example because it is a real consequence of not paying attention.

She also uses numbers. She says Hollis Bend ran 1,140 trips and in 1,137 nobody got hurt. But she says the three that did get hurt matter. This makes the guides see that even a few injuries is a big deal.

At the end she asks "Who sits in your boat?" and lists a welder, a nine-year-old, and a father. This makes the guides think about the passengers and feel responsible. Her last line says to read the river as if lives depend on it. Overall Tenney's choices work together to persuade the guides to be humble and pay attention.

annotations.quote: This shows she has been a guide for a long time so the new guides will listen to her.
annotations.comment: Identifies ethos accurately but does not note that her admission of past overconfidence is what makes her credible to overconfident listeners; commentary is one general sentence.

annotations.quote: The repetition helps the guides remember it.
annotations.comment: Labels the parallelism and gives a generic effect without explaining why the technical lesson comes first or how it works on these listeners.

annotations.quote: This story is sad and makes the audience feel bad, so they will see that strength is not enough.
annotations.comment: Right evidence (Ollie Brask) but the commentary is a vague emotional claim that could fit any passage; it misses the short sentence and the concession about strength.

annotations.quote: Overall Tenney's choices work together to persuade the guides to be humble and pay attention.
annotations.comment: The conclusion repeats the prompt and the essay never explains the movement of the speech or the tension between respecting strength and undercutting confidence, so no sophistication.

blueprint.theme: Attentiveness, humility, and responsibility for others in skilled physical work
blueprint.issue: Whether strength and confidence or watchfulness and humility keep passengers safe on a river
stances: Reading water and practiced humility outweigh strength (speaker's stance)
Strength and quick reflexes are the main safeguard (the audience's implied stance, conceded then rebutted)

devices.function: Establishes experience and models the humility being taught through confession of early overconfidence.
Lists pillow, seam, tongue to make reading water concrete and teachable.
Patterned clauses make the signs and the procedures memorable and rhythmic.
River as self-rewriting sentence frames guiding as continuous reading; recurs to close the speech.
Grants that strength matters, then shows its limits so the audience accepts the correction.
Ollie Brask's failure proves strength cannot replace attention and introduces the moral cost.
Abrupt short sentences deliver verdicts and consequences with force.
A near-perfect safety record is reframed as three harmed families.
Quiet days versus the loud one fixes the standard by which guides are judged.
Redefines humility as procedure, converting virtue into actions.
River with memory and temper, then an indifferent river, places responsibility entirely on the guide.
Turns attention from the guides to their passengers.
Specific passengers make the trust placed in guides concrete and emotionally weighty.
Moves from instruction to stern reckoning to tenderness to imperative, carrying the audience through knowledge, fear, care, and habit.
Closing imperatives give the guides actionable habits tied to the earlier vocabulary.
